```{python}
import torch

from statsforecast import StatsForecast

from statsforecast.models import AutoARIMA, AutoETS, AutoTheta, SeasonalNaive
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPRegressor
from great_tables import GT, loc, style as gt_style
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap, to_hex
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, FancyBboxPatch
import time
from pathlib import Path

CACHE = Path("../cache/09")   # trained results, gitignored; delete a file to recompute it


def cached(name, compute):
    """Load a saved result, or compute it once and save it."""
    path = CACHE / f"{name}.pkl"
    if path.exists():
        return pd.read_pickle(path)
    start = time.time()
    result = compute()
    CACHE.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    pd.to_pickle(result, path)
    with open(CACHE / "timings.log", "a") as log:
        device = "GPU" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "CPU"
        print(f"{name}: {time.time() - start:.1f} s on {device}", file=log)
    return result


shade = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("shade", ["#bfe0b0", "#ffffff", "#f5b8cb"])


def scoreboard(table, rules=None, by="column", decimals=3):
    """A results table in Great Tables: green is better, pink is worse, the best in bold.

    rules maps a metric to "lower", "higher" or a target value (default: every column "lower").
    by="column" compares the rows of each column; by="row" shades each metric on one scale
    and bolds the best of each row.
    """
    df = table.to_frame() if isinstance(table, pd.Series) else table.copy()
    df.index = [str(i) for i in df.index]
    nested = isinstance(df.columns, pd.MultiIndex)
    groups = list(dict.fromkeys(df.columns.get_level_values(0))) if nested else []
    df.columns = ["|".join(map(str, c)) if nested else str(c) for c in df.columns]
    metric = {c: c.split("|")[-1] for c in df.columns}
    rules = rules or {m: "lower" for m in metric.values()}

    gt = (GT(df.reset_index(names="row"), rowname_col="row")
          .fmt_number(columns=list(df.select_dtypes("number").columns), decimals=decimals)
          .sub_missing(missing_text="")
          .cols_label(cases=metric)
          .tab_options(table_font_size="0.75em", data_row_padding="4px"))
    for g in groups:
        gt = gt.tab_spanner(label=g, columns=[c for c in df.columns if c.startswith(f"{g}|")])

    for m, rule in rules.items():
        cols = [c for c in df.columns if metric[c] == m]
        values = df[cols].astype(float)
        bad = values if rule == "lower" else -values if rule == "higher" else (values - rule).abs()
        blocks = [bad[[c]] for c in cols] if by == "column" else [bad]
        for block in blocks:
            lo, hi = np.nanmin(block.values), np.nanmax(block.values)
            for c in block.columns:
                for i, b in enumerate(block[c]):
                    if np.isnan(b):
                        continue
                    fill = to_hex(shade((b - lo) / (hi - lo) if hi > lo else 0.0))
                    best = b == (block[c].min() if by == "column" else bad.iloc[i].min())
                    look = [gt_style.fill(color=fill)] + ([gt_style.text(weight="bold")] if best else [])
                    gt = gt.tab_style(style=look, locations=loc.body(columns=c, rows=[i]))
    return gt


def draw_net(ax, layers, labels, colours, title=""):
    """A small fully connected network: one column of circles per layer, every edge drawn."""
    xs = np.linspace(0, 1, len(layers))
    nodes = []
    for x, n, names, colour in zip(xs, layers, labels, colours):
        ys = np.linspace(0.5 + 0.13 * (n - 1), 0.5 - 0.13 * (n - 1), n)
        nodes.append([(x, y) for y in ys])
        for (cx, cy), name in zip(nodes[-1], names):
            ax.add_patch(Circle((cx, cy), 0.045, facecolor="white", edgecolor=colour, linewidth=2, zorder=3))
            ax.text(cx, cy, name, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=11, zorder=4)
    for left, right in zip(nodes[:-1], nodes[1:]):
        for a in left:
            for b in right:
                ax.plot([a[0] + 0.045, b[0] - 0.045], [a[1], b[1]], color="grey", linewidth=0.8, zorder=1)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.1, 1.1)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.axis("off")
    ax.set_title(title)
```

# Where this fits

## Eight weeks of local models {.smaller}

Every model so far has been **local**: fitted to one series, with its own parameters, knowing nothing
about any other series.

| Week | Model | Learns from |
|---|---|---|
| 1, 3 | benchmarks | one series, one rule |
| 2 | decomposition | one series |
| 4 | ETS | one series |
| 5 | regression | one series and its predictors |
| 6, 7 | ARIMA, dynamic regression | one series and its predictors |
| 8 | MSTL, harmonic regression, Prophet, combinations | one series |

Your Track B series has between 56 and 264 observations. Every parameter of your Lab 7 ARIMA was
estimated from those, and nothing else.

## Three ways a network enters forecasting {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
**1. NNAR — a non-linear AR**

The same lags as an AR model, but the forecast is a non-linear function of them. Still **local**: one
series, its own weights.
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
**2. NeuralProphet — Prophet with lags**

Week 8's trend, seasons and events, plus an **autoregressive network** — the error dynamics Prophet
was missing.
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
**3. Global networks**

One model trained on **many series at once**: LightGBM on lags, then the `neuralforecast` zoo — MLP,
LSTM, TCN, DeepAR, N-BEATS, N-HiTS, TFT, PatchTST, TiDE.
:::
::::

The question for each is the one we have asked for eight weeks: **does it beat the benchmark on a
holdout it never saw?** Next lecture takes the last step — **pretrained** models that forecast your
series without being trained on it at all.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Reading

[FPP3 §12.4 neural network models](https://otexts.com/fpp3/nnetar.html) ·
[Triebe et al. (2021), *NeuralProphet*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.15397) ·

# Neural network autoregression

## An AR model is a network with no hidden layer {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
$$
\hat y_t = c + \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \phi_2 y_{t-2} + \phi_3 y_{t-3}
$$

| Time series | Neural networks |
|---|---|
| lags $y_{t-i}$ | inputs |
| coefficients $\phi_i$ | weights |
| intercept $c$ | bias |
| least squares | training on squared loss |

A linear regression on lags **is** a neural network — one with no hidden layer and no activation.
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{python}
#| label: ar-as-net
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4))
draw_net(ax, [3, 1], [["$y_{t-1}$", "$y_{t-2}$", "$y_{t-3}$"], [r"$\hat y_t$"]],
         [blue, red_pink], "AR(3): inputs straight to the output")
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

## Add a hidden layer {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Each hidden neuron takes its own weighted sum of the lags and squeezes it through a non-linear
**activation**:

$$
\begin{aligned}
z_j &= b_j + \sum_{i=1}^{p} w_{ij}\, y_{t-i}\\[2pt]
h_j &= s(z_j) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z_j}}\\[2pt]
\hat y_t &= a + \sum_{j=1}^{k} v_j\, h_j
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
#| label: nnar-net
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.6))
draw_net(ax, [3, 4, 1], [["$y_{t-1}$", "$y_{t-2}$", "$y_{t-3}$"], ["$h_1$", "$h_2$", "$h_3$", "$h_4$"],
                         [r"$\hat y_t$"]],
         [blue, turquoise, red_pink], "NNAR(3, 4): one hidden layer")
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

$k$ hidden neurons, each a different "view" of the lags. The sigmoid is what makes the model
non-linear — without it the network collapses back to an AR model. Weights start at random values and
are fitted by gradient descent on the squared error.

## NNAR$(p, P, k)_m$ {.smaller}

The model in FPP3 §12.4 — `nnetar()` in R — is exactly this network, with conventions that make it a
forecasting method:

- **Inputs:** $p$ ordinary lags $y_{t-1}, \dots, y_{t-p}$ and $P$ seasonal lags $y_{t-m}, \dots, y_{t-Pm}$.
- **Hidden layer:** one, with $k$ neurons. Default $k = (p + P + 1)/2$, rounded.
- **Defaults for $p$:** the order of the best AR model on the seasonally adjusted series; $P = 1$.
- **Twenty networks**, each from different random starting weights, and their forecasts **averaged**
  — a combination (Week 8) used to tame the randomness of training.
- Inputs are **scaled** first; a network trains badly on raw values in the thousands.

NNAR$(p, 0, k)$ is the non-seasonal version — the one we fit next.

## Sunspots: a non-linear series {.smaller}

The yearly mean number of sunspots, 1700–2008 — Yule fitted the first autoregressive model to this
series in 1927.

```{python}
#| label: sunspots
#| fig-align: center
spots = sm.datasets.sunspots.load_pandas().data
spots["year"] = spots["YEAR"].astype(int)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.4), width_ratios=[2.2, 1])
axes[0].plot(spots["year"], spots["SUNACTIVITY"], color=slate, linewidth=1)
axes[0].set_title("Yearly sunspot number")
cycle = spots.query("1933 <= year <= 1944")
axes[1].plot(cycle["year"], cycle["SUNACTIVITY"], "o-", color=red_pink)
axes[1].set_title("One cycle: up in 4 years, down in 7")
plt.show()
```

The cycles are **asymmetric** — a fast rise, a slow decline — and peaks vary in height. A linear AR
model produces only symmetric cycles: up and down are the same equation.

## Fitting NNAR(9, 5) by hand {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
y_ss = np.sqrt(spots["SUNACTIVITY"].to_numpy())    # square root keeps the forecasts positive
H_SS = 30
train_ss, test_ss = y_ss[:-H_SS], y_ss[-H_SS:]
p, k = 9, 5
mu, sd = train_ss.mean(), train_ss.std()
z = (train_ss - mu) / sd                            # scale the inputs


def lag_matrix(z, p):
    X = np.column_stack([z[p - i - 1:len(z) - i - 1] for i in range(p)])   # y_{t-1}, ..., y_{t-p}
    return X, z[p:]


X, target = lag_matrix(z, p)
nets = [MLPRegressor(hidden_layer_sizes=(k,), activation="logistic", alpha=1e-3,
                     max_iter=5000, random_state=seed).fit(X, target)
        for seed in range(20)]                                             # twenty networks
print(f"{len(target)} training rows, {p} inputs, {k} hidden neurons, "
      f"{p * k + k + k + 1} weights per network")
```

## Forecasting: one step at a time {.smaller}

A network predicts **one step ahead**. For $h > 1$ the forecast is fed back as if it were data — the
same recursion as ARIMA, but through a non-linear function:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
def nnar_forecast(nets, z, h, noise=None, rng=None):
    history, out = list(z[-p:]), []
    for _ in range(h):
        x = np.array(history[::-1][:p])[None, :]               # the latest p values, newest first
        value = np.mean([net.predict(x)[0] for net in nets])   # average of the twenty networks
        if noise is not None:
            value += rng.choice(noise)                         # a resampled training error
        out.append(value)
        history.append(value)
    return np.array(out)


point_ss = (nnar_forecast(nets, z, H_SS) * sd + mu) ** 2      # back to the sunspot scale
```

There is no formula for the forecast variance of a non-linear model. FPP's answer: **simulate**. Add a
resampled training error at every step, repeat many times, and read the interval off the paths.

## The simulated paths {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: nnar-paths
#| fig-align: center
residuals_ss = target - np.mean([net.predict(X) for net in nets], axis=0)
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
paths_ss = cached("nnar-paths", lambda: np.array(
    [(nnar_forecast(nets, z, H_SS, residuals_ss, rng) * sd + mu) ** 2 for _ in range(300)]))
lo80, hi80 = np.percentile(paths_ss, [10, 90], axis=0)
years_test = spots["year"].to_numpy()[-H_SS:]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.8))
ax.plot(spots["year"], spots["SUNACTIVITY"], color=slate, linewidth=1, label="sunspots")
for path in paths_ss[:12]:
    ax.plot(years_test, path, color=turquoise, alpha=0.35, linewidth=0.8)
ax.fill_between(years_test, lo80, hi80, color=red_pink, alpha=0.18, label="80% of 300 paths")
ax.plot(years_test, point_ss, color=red_pink, linewidth=2, label="NNAR(9, 5) forecast")
ax.set_xlim(1900, 2009)
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
ax.set_title("Thirty years ahead from 1978: twelve of the simulated paths, and the interval from all of them")
plt.show()
```

Three cycles ahead, the forecast keeps their **timing** (about 11 years) but not their **height** —
averaging damps every peak to about 100 — nor their **shape**: it rises for about 5 years and falls
for 5.5, where the real cycles rise for 4.5 and fall for 6.4.

## Scored on the thirty held-out years {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| output-location: column
arima_ss = AutoARIMA().fit(train_ss)
ets_ss = AutoETS().fit(train_ss)
truth = test_ss ** 2
candidates_ss = {
    "NNAR(9, 5)": point_ss,
    str(ARIMASummary(arima_ss.model_)): arima_ss.predict(H_SS)["mean"] ** 2,
    "AutoETS": ets_ss.predict(H_SS)["mean"] ** 2,
    "mean of the training years": np.full(H_SS, (train_ss ** 2).mean()),
}
scoreboard(pd.DataFrame({
    name: {"MAE": np.mean(np.abs(truth - f)),
           "RMSE": np.sqrt(np.mean((truth - f) ** 2))}
    for name, f in candidates_ss.items()}).T, decimals=1)
```

- The network's error is about **a third lower** than the ARIMA's — both fitted on the same
  square-root scale, both forecasting 30 years.
- ETS, which has no cycles at all, does no better than the mean of the training years.
- This is the case NNAR was built for: a **long** series (270 training rows) with **genuinely
  non-linear** dynamics.

## What NNAR is, and is not {.smaller}

- **Is:** an autoregression that can bend. When the dynamics are genuinely non-linear — asymmetric
  cycles, thresholds, saturation — it can see what a linear model cannot.
- **Is not:** interpretable. 56 weights per network, twenty networks; there is no $\phi_1$ to read.
- **Is not:** stable without care. Different seeds give different networks; that is why it averages
  twenty.
- **Is not:** data-efficient. Sunspots give 300 years; your Track B series gives 56 to 264
  observations, and a network with 56 weights per 100 points is fitting noise.

[That last point is the real limit of a local network — and the reason the last part of this lecture
trains on many series at once.]{.hi}

# From Prophet to NeuralProphet

## What Prophet was missing {.smaller}

Week 8's verdict on Prophet: a convenient regression — piecewise trend, Fourier seasons, holiday
windows — with **no error dynamics**. It never looks at yesterday. Its intervals were too narrow, and on
cement and electricity it lost to seasonal naive.

**NeuralProphet** (Triebe et al., 2021) keeps Prophet's decomposition and adds what was missing:

$$
\hat y_t = \underbrace{T(t) + S(t) + E(t) + F(t)}_{\text{Prophet's terms}} \; + \;
\underbrace{A(t)}_{\text{AR-Net}} \; + \; \underbrace{L(t)}_{\text{lagged regressors}}
$$

- $T, S, E, F$: trend, Fourier seasonality, events, future regressors — as in Prophet.
- $A(t)$: an **autoregression on the last $p$ values**, fitted as a small network — AR-Net. With no
  hidden layer it is a linear AR($p$); with hidden layers it is NNAR.
- $L(t)$: lags of other series — Week 7's lagged predictors.
- Everything is fitted together in **PyTorch**, by stochastic gradient descent, not by Stan.

## The same interface {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| eval: false
from neuralprophet import NeuralProphet

m = NeuralProphet(n_lags=14,          # AR-Net: the last 14 days as inputs
                  n_forecasts=7)      # one output per step: 7 days ahead, directly
m = m.add_future_regressor("tournament")
m.fit(train[["ds", "y", "tournament"]], freq="D")
forecast = m.predict(test[["ds", "y", "tournament"]])   # yhat1 ... yhat7
```

- `n_forecasts=7` makes the forecast **direct**: one output neuron per horizon, not a recursion as in
  NNAR. Column `yhat3` is the forecast made three days earlier.
- Without `n_lags` the model is Prophet refitted by gradient descent — a useful check that nothing
  else has changed.

::: {.callout-warning}
## A package to use with care

NeuralProphet's last release is **0.9.0, June 2024**. It requires `numpy < 2` and `pandas < 3`, so it does
not install into this course's environment, and in Colab it downgrades numpy. The results on the next
slides were computed in a separate environment by `infra/neuralprophet_messi.py`; the deck reads them.
:::

## Messi again: one year, seven horizons {.smaller}

Week 8's page views, on logs. Every model is **fitted once**, on the history to 30 September 2025, with
the same tournament flag; the following year is the test. The AR-Net uses the actual views up to each
forecast origin — that is what an autoregression does — but is never refitted. MAE on log views;
naive $= y_{t-h}$, snaive $= y_{t-7}$, NP $=$ NeuralProphet.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| output-location: column
np_messi = pd.read_csv("../data/neuralprophet_messi.csv",
                       parse_dates=["ds"]).dropna()
views = pd.read_csv("../data/messi_wikipedia.csv",
                    parse_dates=["ds"]).set_index("ds")["y"]
log_views = np.log(views)
y_np = np_messi.set_index("ds")["y"]
mae = lambda f: float(np.mean(np.abs(y_np - f)))
by_h = pd.DataFrame({f"h={h}": {
    "naive": mae(log_views.shift(h).reindex(y_np.index)),
    "snaive": mae(log_views.shift(7).reindex(y_np.index)),
    "AR-Net": mae(np_messi.set_index("ds")[f"AR-Net h={h}"]),
    "NP, no lags": mae(np_messi.set_index("ds")["NeuralProphet"]),
    "Prophet": mae(np_messi.set_index("ds")["Prophet"]),
} for h in range(1, 8)}).T
scoreboard(by_h, by="row")
```

## What the lags bought {.smaller}

- **Prophet and NeuralProphet without lags lose to seasonal naive** at every horizon: on daily
  attention data, "same day last week" knows more than any smooth trend and season. Refitting Prophet
  by gradient descent helps a little, not enough — the missing piece was never the optimiser.
- **The AR-Net closes most of that gap.** Its error at 7 days is less than two thirds of Prophet's.
- **One day ahead it is no better than naive.** "Same as yesterday" is very hard to beat at $h = 1$; the
  AR-Net's advantage grows with the horizon, to about 12% at $h = 7$.

```{python}
#| label: np-world-cup
#| fig-align: center
window = np_messi[np_messi["ds"].between("2026-05-15", "2026-08-15")]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.1))
ax.plot(window["ds"], window["y"], color=slate, linewidth=1.3, label="actual")
for col, colour, style in [("Prophet", turquoise, "-"), ("NeuralProphet", blue, "-"),
                           ("AR-Net h=7", orange, "-"), ("AR-Net h=1", red_pink, "--")]:
    ax.plot(window["ds"], window[col], style, color=colour, linewidth=1.5, label=col)
ax.axvspan(pd.Timestamp("2026-06-11"), pd.Timestamp("2026-07-19"), color=orange, alpha=0.08)
ax.set_ylabel("log views")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8, ncol=5)
ax.set_title("The 2026 World Cup: models without lags cannot follow the matches; the AR-Net follows them a step behind")
plt.show()
```

## Inside the AR-Net {.smaller}

With no hidden layer the AR-Net is a $7 \times 14$ matrix: one row of lag weights per horizon.

```{python}
#| label: ar-weights
#| fig-align: center
weights = pd.read_csv("../data/neuralprophet_ar_weights.csv", index_col=0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.2))
image = ax.imshow(weights.to_numpy(), cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-0.5, vmax=0.5, aspect="auto")
ax.set_xticks(range(14), [c.replace("lag ", "") for c in weights.columns])
ax.set_yticks(range(7), weights.index)
ax.set_xlabel("lag (days before the forecast origin)")
fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, shrink=0.8)
ax.set_title("AR-Net weights: rows are horizons, columns are lags")
plt.show()
```

The largest weights are on **lag 14** — the same weekday two weeks back — and the signs alternate from
lag to lag. This is not an ARIMA $\phi$ you can read: correlated lags share the work in arbitrary ways.
NeuralProphet buys accuracy here, not a cleaner story.

# Global models

## Local and global {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Local** — one model per series

- $N$ series → $N$ sets of parameters.
- Each set is estimated from one series.
- ETS, ARIMA, NNAR, Prophet.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Global** — one model for all

- $N$ series → **one** set of parameters.
- Estimated from every window of every series.
- A seasonal shape seen in 500 series helps forecast the 501st.
:::
::::

A global model needs the series to be **comparable**, so each one is scaled by its own level first.
After that, it learns "what happens after a pattern like this", pooled over everything it has seen.

Evidence from the competitions: in **M4** (2018) the winner was a hybrid — exponential smoothing inside a
recurrent network trained across series — and the pure machine-learning entries did worse than the
statistical benchmarks. In **M5** (2020), on tens of thousands of Walmart series, the top of the
leaderboard was dominated by **LightGBM** trained globally.

## The data for this section: M3 Monthly {.smaller}

The 1428 monthly series of the **M3 competition** (Makridakis & Hibon, 2000) — micro, industry, macro,
finance, demographic — each with its last **18 months** held out, as in the competition.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
m3 = pd.read_csv("../data/m3_monthly.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
H_M3 = 18
test_m3 = m3.groupby("unique_id").tail(H_M3)
train_m3 = m3.drop(test_m3.index)
lengths = train_m3.groupby("unique_id").size()
print(f"{m3['unique_id'].nunique()} series; training length {lengths.min()} to {lengths.max()} months, "
      f"median {lengths.median():.0f}")
```

Every model in the rest of this lecture is scored on these same 1428 × 18 held-out months, by MASE with
$m = 12$ — the metric you have used since Week 3.

## The local baseline {.smaller}

Three local models, 1428 fits each — and the Week 8 combination of two of them:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| eval: false
local = StatsForecast(models=[SeasonalNaive(season_length=12, alias="snaive"),
                              AutoETS(season_length=12, alias="ETS"),
                              AutoTheta(season_length=12, alias="Theta")],
                      freq="MS")
forecasts = test_m3.merge(local.forecast(df=train_m3, h=H_M3), on=["unique_id", "ds"])
forecasts["ETS + Theta"] = (forecasts["ETS"] + forecasts["Theta"]) / 2
```

```{python}
#| include: false
local = StatsForecast(models=[SeasonalNaive(season_length=12, alias="snaive"),
                              AutoETS(season_length=12, alias="ETS"),
                              AutoTheta(season_length=12, alias="Theta")],
                      freq="MS")
forecasts = test_m3.merge(cached("m3-local", lambda: local.forecast(df=train_m3, h=H_M3)), on=["unique_id", "ds"])
forecasts["ETS + Theta"] = (forecasts["ETS"] + forecasts["Theta"]) / 2
```

The **Theta** method won M3 in 2000. It is simple exponential smoothing with drift — Week 4 — on a
seasonally adjusted series, and it remains one of the hardest benchmarks to beat on this data.

```{python}
#| include: false
scale_m3 = train_m3.groupby("unique_id")["y"].apply(lambda s: np.mean(np.abs(s.to_numpy()[12:] - s.to_numpy()[:-12])))


def m3_board(columns):
    err = forecasts.groupby("unique_id").apply(
        lambda g: pd.Series({c: np.mean(np.abs(g["y"] - g[c])) for c in columns}), include_groups=False)
    mase_m3 = err.div(scale_m3, axis=0)
    return pd.DataFrame({"mean MASE": mase_m3.mean(), "median MASE": mase_m3.median(),
                         "beats ETS on": mase_m3.lt(mase_m3["ETS"], axis=0).mean()})
```

## A global LightGBM on lags {.smaller}

The M5 recipe: a gradient-boosted tree model, **one** for all 1428 series, on lag features. Week 7's
dynamic regression with the lags as predictors — except that a tree finds the non-linearities itself.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
from mlforecast import MLForecast
from mlforecast.target_transforms import Differences, LocalStandardScaler
import lightgbm as lgb

boosted = MLForecast(
    models={"LightGBM": lgb.LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.05, verbose=-1)},
    freq="MS",
    lags=[1, 2, 3, 6, 12, 24],                                   # the features
    date_features=["month"],
    target_transforms=[Differences([12]), LocalStandardScaler()],   # D = 1, then each series scaled
)
boosted.fit(train_m3)
forecasts = forecasts.merge(boosted.predict(H_M3), on=["unique_id", "ds"])
```

- `Differences([12])` is Week 7's seasonal difference; `LocalStandardScaler` puts every series on one
  scale, which is what makes **pooling** them possible.
- Forecasts are recursive, as for NNAR: each prediction becomes a lag for the next.

One reasonable configuration, the kind you would try first — **not tuned**. Tuning a global model is a
project of its own; the next slides show what you get on the first attempt.

## LightGBM, scored {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
board_lgb = m3_board(["snaive", "ETS", "Theta", "ETS + Theta", "LightGBM"])
scoreboard(board_lgb, rules={"mean MASE": "lower", "median MASE": "lower", "beats ETS on": "higher"})
```
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{python}
#| label: lgb-vs-ets
#| fig-align: center
err_m3 = forecasts.groupby("unique_id").apply(
    lambda g: pd.Series({c: np.mean(np.abs(g["y"] - g[c])) for c in ["ETS", "LightGBM"]}),
    include_groups=False).div(scale_m3, axis=0)
ratio = err_m3["LightGBM"] / err_m3["ETS"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.0))
ax.hist(np.log2(ratio), bins=np.arange(-4, 4.01, 0.25), color=red_pink, alpha=0.8)
ax.axvline(0, color="black", linewidth=1)
ax.set_xticks(range(-4, 5), ["1/16", "1/8", "1/4", "1/2", "1", "2", "4", "8", "16"])
ax.set_xlabel("MASE of LightGBM / MASE of ETS, per series (log scale)")
ax.set_ylabel("series")
ax.set_title(f"LightGBM better on {np.mean(ratio < 1):.0%} of the series, worse on {np.mean(ratio > 1):.0%}",
             fontsize=10)
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

- **Better than "same month last year", worse than every local model.** One model for 1428 series
  beats ETS on only a third of them.
- **The losses are bigger than the wins:** ETS is more than twice as accurate on about one series in
  five; LightGBM is, on about one in fourteen.

## What the trees learned, and where they fail {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: lgb-inside
#| fig-align: center
gain = pd.Series(boosted.models_["LightGBM"].booster_.feature_importance("gain"),
                 index=boosted.ts.features_order_).sort_values()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(14, 3.6), width_ratios=[0.8, 1, 1, 1])
axes[0].barh(gain.index, gain / gain.sum(), color=slate)
axes[0].xaxis.set_major_formatter(mpl.ticker.PercentFormatter(1.0))
axes[0].set_title("Share of the split gain", fontsize=10)
for ax, uid in zip(axes[1:], ["M1072", "M106", "M854"]):
    hist = train_m3[train_m3["unique_id"] == uid].tail(48)
    fut = forecasts[forecasts["unique_id"] == uid]
    ax.plot(hist["ds"], hist["y"], color=slate, linewidth=1)
    ax.plot(fut["ds"], fut["y"], color="black", linewidth=1, label="actual")
    ax.plot(fut["ds"], fut["LightGBM"], color=red_pink, linewidth=1.8, label="LightGBM")
    ax.plot(fut["ds"], fut["ETS"], "--", color=blue, linewidth=1.3, label="ETS")
    ax.set_title(f"{uid}: LightGBM / ETS MASE = {ratio[uid]:.2f}", fontsize=10)
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=8)
axes[1].legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

- **Mostly the last month.** `lag1` carries over half of the gain, `lag12` comes second; `month` is
  almost unused, because `Differences([12])` has already removed the seasonal shape.
- **M1072:** a steady trend — LightGBM carries it on, ETS damps it. **M106:** noise around a level;
  ETS forecasts the level, LightGBM chases the wiggles.
- **M854:** a series that turned down. Its recent changes are unlike its own past, the trees have no leaf
  for them, and the forecast jumps back up. **A tree cannot predict a value outside what it saw** —
  the extrapolation that ETS's trend does for free.

# The neuralforecast model zoo

## How `neuralforecast` trains every model {.smaller}

Every model in [`neuralforecast`](https://nixtlaverse.nixtla.io/neuralforecast/) learns from the same
kind of example: a **window** of `input_size` past values and the `h` values that follow, cut at a
random point of a random series.

```{python}
#| label: windows
#| fig-align: center
air = pd.read_csv("../data/air_passengers.csv", parse_dates=["ds"]).assign(unique_id="air")
example = air["y"].to_numpy()[:120]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 2.6), sharey=True)
for ax, start in zip(axes, [5, 35, 70]):
    ax.plot(example, color="lightgray", linewidth=1)
    ax.plot(range(start, start + 24), example[start:start + 24], color=blue, linewidth=2, label="input: 24 values")
    ax.plot(range(start + 24, start + 42), example[start + 24:start + 42], color=red_pink, linewidth=2,
            label="target: the next 18")
    ax.set_xticks([])
axes[0].legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
fig.suptitle("Three training examples from one series; a batch mixes windows from many series", fontsize=11)
plt.show()
```

- **Scaling** (`scaler_type`): each window is scaled by its own level and spread, so a series in the
  millions and a series in the tens can share one set of weights.
- **Loss** (`loss`): MAE by default; a distribution or quantile loss gives intervals.
- **Training** (`max_steps`): that many batches of windows, by gradient descent. Forecasting is one
  forward pass on the last window of each series.

## Four families {.smaller}

| Family | Models | How it reads the window |
|---|---|---|
| **Fully connected** | MLP, N-BEATS, N-HiTS, TiDE | all 24 values at once, as one input vector |
| **Recurrent** | RNN, LSTM, GRU, DeepAR | one value at a time, carrying a state forward |
| **Convolutional** | TCN | sliding filters over neighbouring values |
| **Attention** | TFT, PatchTST | every position weighs every other |

: {tbl-colwidths="[18,30,52]"}

The simplest is the **MLP**: the window goes in as a vector, through hidden layers with ReLU, and
**all 18 forecasts come out at once** — a direct forecast, not NNAR's recursion:

$$
\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{T+1:T+h} = W_2\, \text{ReLU}\!\left(W_1\, \mathbf{y}_{T-23:T} + b_1\right) + b_2
$$

NNAR from the first section, made global and multi-output. Every other model in this section is a
more careful way of turning the window into those $h$ numbers.

## Recurrent networks: a memory that is carried forward {.smaller}

NNAR sees a **fixed window** of $p$ lags. A recurrent network (RNN) reads the series one value at a time
and carries a **hidden state** $h_t$ — a vector summary of everything so far:

$$
h_t = \tanh\left(W h_{t-1} + U y_t + b\right), \qquad \hat y_{t+1} = V h_t + c
$$

```{python}
#| label: rnn-unrolled
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 2.1))
for i, t in enumerate(["t-2", "t-1", "t", "t+1"]):
    x = i * 2.2
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x, 0.8), 1.2, 0.8, boxstyle="round,pad=0.05", facecolor="white",
                                edgecolor=turquoise, linewidth=2))
    ax.text(x + 0.6, 1.2, f"$h_{{{t}}}$", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13)
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x + 0.6, 0.78), xytext=(x + 0.6, 0.1), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=blue))
    ax.text(x + 0.6, -0.05, f"$y_{{{t}}}$", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=13)
    if i < 3:
        ax.annotate("", xy=(x + 2.18, 1.2), xytext=(x + 1.27, 1.2), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=red_pink, lw=2))
        ax.text(x + 1.72, 1.32, "$W$", color=red_pink, fontsize=12, ha="center")
ax.set_xlim(-0.3, 8.2)
ax.set_ylim(-0.5, 1.8)
ax.axis("off")
ax.set_title("The same weights $W, U$ at every step: the network unrolled through time")
plt.show()
```

No fixed window, and the **same** weights at every step — as ARIMA's recursion is to a regression on
fixed lags.

## Why RNNs forget, and how LSTM remembers {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: lstm-cell
#| fig-align: center
cell_c, hidden_c = "#2e8b57", red_pink
fig, (ax, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13.5, 4.4), width_ratios=[2.7, 1])
ax.set_xlim(-0.6, 14.6)
ax.set_ylim(-0.2, 8.4)
ax.axis("off")
ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((1.2, 0.6), 12.4, 7.0, boxstyle="round,pad=0.1", facecolor="#f4f4f4",
                            edgecolor="#cccccc", zorder=0))


def arrow(x0, y0, x1, y1, colour="grey", width=1.6):
    ax.annotate("", (x1, y1), (x0, y0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=colour, lw=width,
                                                        shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0), zorder=2)


def node(x, y, sign, colour):
    ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), 0.3, facecolor="white", edgecolor=colour, lw=2, zorder=3))
    ax.text(x, y, sign, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color=colour, zorder=4)


def gate(x, y, name, colour, label):
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x - 0.55, y - 0.4), 1.1, 0.8, boxstyle="round,pad=0.04",
                                facecolor="white", edgecolor=colour, lw=2, zorder=3))
    ax.text(x, y, name, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=12, zorder=4)
    ax.text(x, y - 0.68, label, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=9, color=colour, fontweight="bold")


# the cell state: long-term memory, a highway with only x and +
ax.plot([-0.4, 14.4], [7, 7], color=cell_c, lw=4, zorder=1)
arrow(14.0, 7, 14.5, 7, cell_c, 4)
ax.text(-0.4, 7.35, "$c_{t-1}$", fontsize=13, color=cell_c)
ax.text(13.9, 7.35, "$c_t$", fontsize=13, color=cell_c)
ax.text(7.2, 8.05, "cell state = long-term memory: only scaled (×) and added to (+)", ha="center",
        fontsize=10, color=cell_c, fontweight="bold")
# the hidden state: short-term memory
ax.plot([-0.4, 3.0], [1.2, 1.2], color=hidden_c, lw=3, zorder=1)
ax.plot([3.0, 3.0, 11.0], [1.2, 2.3, 2.3], color="grey", lw=1.8, zorder=1)        # [h, y] bus
ax.text(-0.4, 1.5, "$h_{t-1}$", fontsize=13, color=hidden_c)
arrow(3.0, -0.15, 3.0, 2.3, slate, 2)
ax.text(2.85, -0.05, "this month $y_t$", ha="right", fontsize=10, color=slate)
# four gates read [h_{t-1}, y_t]
for x, name, colour, label in [(4.4, r"$\sigma$", blue, "forget $f_t$"), (6.5, r"$\sigma$", orange, "input $i_t$"),
                               (8.6, "tanh", purple, "candidate"), (10.7, r"$\sigma$", red_pink, "output $o_t$")]:
    ax.plot([x, x], [2.3, 3.6], color="grey", lw=1.8, zorder=1)
    gate(x, 4.0, name, colour, label)
# forget: scale the old memory
arrow(4.4, 4.4, 4.4, 6.7, blue)
node(4.4, 7, "×", blue)
ax.text(4.6, 5.6, "keep how much\nof the old?", fontsize=9, color=blue)
# input x candidate: what to write, added to the memory
ax.plot([6.5, 6.5, 7.25], [4.4, 5.5, 5.5], color=orange, lw=1.6, zorder=1)
ax.plot([8.6, 8.6, 7.85], [4.4, 5.5, 5.5], color=purple, lw=1.6, zorder=1)
node(7.55, 5.5, "×", orange)
arrow(7.55, 5.8, 7.55, 6.7, orange)
node(7.55, 7, "+", cell_c)
ax.text(7.85, 6.05, "write\nsomething new", fontsize=9, color=orange)
# output: read a filtered memory into h_t
ax.plot([12.4, 12.4], [7, 5.9], color=cell_c, lw=1.6, zorder=1)
gate(12.4, 5.5, "tanh", cell_c, "")
arrow(12.4, 5.1, 12.4, 4.3, cell_c)
arrow(11.25, 4.0, 12.1, 4.0, red_pink)
node(12.4, 4.0, "×", red_pink)
ax.text(12.6, 3.3, "show\nhow much?", fontsize=9, color=red_pink)
ax.plot([12.4, 12.4, 14.0], [3.7, 1.2, 1.2], color=hidden_c, lw=3, zorder=1)
arrow(14.0, 1.2, 14.5, 1.2, hidden_c, 3)
ax.text(13.9, 1.5, "$h_t$", fontsize=13, color=hidden_c)
ax.text(8.3, 0.2, "hidden state = short-term memory; the forecast is read from it", ha="center",
        fontsize=10, color=hidden_c, fontweight="bold")
# why a plain RNN forgets
steps = np.arange(0, 25)
ax2.plot(steps, 0.75 ** steps, "o-", color=slate, ms=3, label="plain RNN: ×0.75 per step")
ax2.plot(steps, 0.98 ** steps, "o-", color=cell_c, ms=3, label="LSTM cell: $f_t$ = 0.98")
ax2.axvline(12, color="grey", linestyle="--", lw=1)
ax2.text(12.4, 0.5, "last\nDecember", fontsize=9, color="grey")
ax2.set_xlabel("steps back in time")
ax2.set_title("How much of a month's signal\nis left after $k$ steps", fontsize=10)
ax2.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper right")
plt.show()
```

- **Plain RNN:** the whole state is rewritten every step, so last December's signal is squeezed twelve
  times and almost gone (right) — in training, the **vanishing gradient**.
- **LSTM** (1997) adds the green line, a memory that is only **scaled and added to**. Three sigmoid gates
  decide what to forget, write and show; with $f_t \approx 1$ the memory survives — ETS's level, learned.
  **GRU** (2014): the same idea, two gates, no separate cell.

## TCN: convolutions that only look back {.smaller}

A **temporal convolutional network** (Bai, Kolter & Koltun, 2018) slides small filters along the series —
Week 2's moving average, with learned weights and a non-linearity, stacked in layers.

```{python}
#| label: tcn
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3))
n, dilations = 16, [1, 2, 4]                  # layer l+1 combines t and t - dilations[l] of layer l
reach = {3: {15}}
for layer in (2, 1, 0):
    reach[layer] = {s for t in reach[layer + 1] for s in (t, t - dilations[layer])}
for layer in range(4):
    ax.scatter(range(n), [layer] * n, s=40, color="white", edgecolor=slate, zorder=3)
    ax.scatter(sorted(reach[layer]), [layer] * len(reach[layer]), s=60, color=red_pink, zorder=4)
for layer, d in enumerate(dilations):
    for t in range(d, n):
        on_path = t in reach[layer + 1]
        for src in (t, t - d):
            ax.plot([src, t], [layer, layer + 1], color=red_pink if on_path else "lightgray",
                    linewidth=1.4 if on_path else 0.6, zorder=2 if on_path else 1)
ax.set_yticks(range(4), ["input", "dilation 1", "dilation 2", "dilation 4 → output"])
ax.set_xticks([])
ax.set_title("Each output sees only the past (causal), and the reach doubles with every layer (dilated)")
plt.show()
```

- **Causal**: the filter at time $t$ uses only $t, t-1, \dots$ — never the future.
- **Dilated**: layer $\ell$ skips $2^{\ell}$ steps, so a few layers cover a long window — here three
  layers reach eight months back.
- No recurrence, so every position is computed **in parallel**: faster to train than an LSTM.

## DeepAR: a distribution at every step {.smaller}

**DeepAR** (Salinas et al., 2020; Amazon) is a global LSTM whose output is not a number but the
**parameters of a distribution** — here a Student-$t$, $(\mu_t, \sigma_t, \nu_t)$:

$$
y_t \mid y_{1:t-1} \sim t_{\nu_t}\!\left(\mu_t, \sigma_t\right), \qquad (\mu_t, \sigma_t, \nu_t) = g(h_t)
$$

- **Training** maximises the likelihood of the observed values — Week 4's maximum likelihood, with
  an LSTM in place of the ETS equations.
- **Forecasting** samples: draw $y_{T+1}$, feed it back, draw $y_{T+2}$, … Many sample paths give the
  quantiles — the NNAR simulation from the first section, built into the model.
- The interval comes from the model, not from resampled residuals — so it can widen where the
  network has learned that series are volatile.

## N-BEATS: pass on what you cannot explain {.smaller}

**N-BEATS** (Oreshkin et al., 2020): a chain of fully connected blocks. Two of them, on Air Passengers:

```{python}
#| label: nbeats-blocks
#| fig-align: center
window = np.log(air["y"].to_numpy()[-72:-24])           # 48 months in, 24 ahead
future = np.log(air["y"].to_numpy()[-24:])
t = np.arange(72) / 72                                     # one time axis for backcast and forecast
past, ahead = slice(0, 48), slice(48, 72)
trend_basis = np.column_stack([t ** k for k in range(2)])  # 1, t
season_basis = np.column_stack([f(2 * np.pi * k * np.arange(72) / 12) for k in (1, 2) for f in (np.cos, np.sin)])


def block(x, basis):
    theta = np.linalg.lstsq(basis[past], x, rcond=None)[0]   # the network learns theta; here, least squares
    return basis[past] @ theta, basis[ahead] @ theta         # backcast, forecast


trend_back, trend_fore = block(window, trend_basis)
rest = window - trend_back
season_back, season_fore = block(rest, season_basis)
left = rest - season_back

months, horizon = np.arange(48), np.arange(48, 72)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13.5, 3.7), width_ratios=[1.15, 1.15, 1.15])
axes[0].plot(months, window, color=slate, linewidth=1.2, label="input: the window")
axes[0].plot(months, trend_back, color=blue, linewidth=2, label="backcast")
axes[0].plot(horizon, trend_fore, "--", color=blue, linewidth=2, label="forecast")
axes[0].set_title("Block 1 (trend): explains what it can", fontsize=10, color=blue)
axes[1].plot(months, rest, color=slate, linewidth=1.2, label="input: window − block 1's backcast")
axes[1].plot(months, season_back, color=orange, linewidth=2, label="backcast")
axes[1].plot(horizon, season_fore, "--", color=orange, linewidth=2, label="forecast")
axes[1].plot(months, left, ":", color="grey", linewidth=1, label="still unexplained")
axes[1].set_title("Block 2 (season): gets only the rest", fontsize=10, color=orange)
axes[2].plot(months, window, color=slate, linewidth=1.2, label="window")
axes[2].plot(horizon, future, color="black", linewidth=1.2, label="actual")
axes[2].plot(horizon, trend_fore + season_fore, color=red_pink, linewidth=2.2, label="block 1 + block 2")
axes[2].set_title("Forecast = sum of the blocks' forecasts", fontsize=10, color=red_pink)
for ax in axes:
    ax.axvline(47.5, color="grey", linewidth=0.8)
    ax.set_xlabel("month")
    ax.legend(fontsize=7.5, loc="best")
axes[0].set_ylabel("log passengers")
for x in (0.345, 0.66):
    fig.text(x, 0.5, "→", fontsize=24, color="grey", ha="center", va="center")
plt.show()
```

- Each block returns a **backcast** (the part of its input it explains) and a **forecast** of that part,
  then passes on **the rest**. The final forecast is the **sum** of the blocks' forecasts.
- Real N-BEATS stacks dozens of blocks whose layers learn the coefficients (least squares here, for the
  mechanics). **Interpretable** blocks are fixed to trend and Fourier terms (Week 5). It beat M4's winner.

## Not just a decomposition {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: nbeats-vs-decomposition
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(13.5, 5.0))
ax.set_xlim(0, 27)
ax.set_ylim(0, 9.4)
ax.axis("off")


def card(x, y, w, h, text, colour, filled=False):
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x, y), w, h, boxstyle="round,pad=0.08", lw=2, edgecolor=colour,
                                facecolor=colour if filled else "white", alpha=1, zorder=2))
    ax.text(x + w / 2, y + h / 2, text, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=14, zorder=3,
            color="white" if filled else "black")


def link(x0, y0, x1, y1, colour="grey"):
    ax.annotate("", (x1, y1), (x0, y0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=colour, lw=1.8), zorder=1)


def note(x, y, text, colour):
    ax.text(x, y, text, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=12.5, color=colour, style="italic")


# decomposition, then a forecast
ax.text(0.1, 9.05, "Decomposition, then a forecast (Weeks 2–4)", fontsize=15, fontweight="bold", color=slate)
card(0.3, 6.3, 3.6, 1.7, "one series\n(all of its past)", slate)
card(5.0, 6.3, 4.2, 1.7, "STL / moving\naverages: smooth\nthe past", slate)
card(10.3, 6.3, 4.6, 1.7, "trend + season\n+ remainder\nof the past", slate)
card(16.0, 6.3, 4.6, 1.7, "a second model per\ncomponent: drift,\nseasonal naive, ETS", slate)
card(21.7, 6.3, 3.6, 1.7, "forecast", slate, filled=True)
for x0, x1 in [(3.9, 5.0), (9.2, 10.3), (14.9, 16.0), (20.6, 21.7)]:
    link(x0, 7.15, x1, 7.15, slate)
note(7.1, 6.05, "fitted to this series only", slate)
note(12.6, 6.05, "describes the past:\njudged by how well it fits", slate)
note(18.3, 6.05, "the future is a\nseparate step", slate)

# N-BEATS
ax.text(0.1, 4.15, "N-BEATS", fontsize=15, fontweight="bold", color=red_pink)
card(0.3, 1.5, 3.6, 1.7, "a window of\nany series", red_pink)
card(5.0, 1.5, 4.2, 1.7, "fully connected\nlayers: the same\nweights for all", red_pink)
card(10.3, 2.45, 4.6, 0.85, "backcast  →  minus", blue)
card(10.3, 1.4, 4.6, 0.85, "forecast  →  plus", orange)
card(16.0, 2.3, 4.6, 1.0, "next block gets\nwhat is left", red_pink)
card(21.7, 1.5, 3.6, 1.7, "forecast =\nsum of blocks", red_pink, filled=True)
link(3.9, 2.35, 5.0, 2.35, red_pink)
link(9.2, 2.85, 10.3, 2.85, red_pink)
link(9.2, 1.85, 10.3, 1.85, red_pink)
link(14.9, 2.85, 16.0, 2.85, blue)
link(14.9, 1.8, 21.7, 1.8, orange)
ax.annotate("", (7.1, 3.25), (18.3, 3.25), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="grey", lw=1.4,
                                                           connectionstyle="arc3,rad=0.25", linestyle="--"))
ax.text(12.6, 4.15, "repeat", fontsize=12.5, color="grey", ha="center")
note(7.1, 1.2, "trained on thousands of windows\nfrom many series", red_pink)
note(12.6, 1.15, "both from one pass", red_pink)
note(18.3, 1.2, "trained on forecast error:\nthe backcast only serves the forecast", red_pink)
plt.show()
```

- **Where the pieces come from:** STL is fitted to one series; N-BEATS's layers read any window and output
  the pieces — one set of weights for all series, no refit for a new one.
- **What is optimised:** a decomposition is judged on the past, N-BEATS only on forecast error — a block
  may describe the past imperfectly if the forecast gains. What is left after the last block is dropped.

## Training the zoo on M3 {.smaller}

The same 1428 series, horizon and windows as LightGBM. Every model with one configuration, its library
defaults plus three shared settings — **nothing tuned**:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| eval: false
from neuralforecast import NeuralForecast
from neuralforecast.models import MLP, LSTM, GRU, TCN, DeepAR, NBEATS, NHITS, TFT, PatchTST, TiDE
from neuralforecast.losses.pytorch import DistributionLoss, MAE
import time

quiet = dict(enable_progress_bar=False, logger=False, enable_model_summary=False)
shared = dict(h=H_M3, input_size=24, scaler_type="robust", max_steps=600, random_seed=1, **quiet)
zoo = {"MLP": MLP(**shared), "LSTM": LSTM(**shared), "GRU": GRU(**shared), "TCN": TCN(**shared),
       "DeepAR": DeepAR(**shared, loss=DistributionLoss("StudentT", level=[80]), valid_loss=MAE()),
       "NBEATS": NBEATS(**shared), "NHITS": NHITS(**shared), "TFT": TFT(**shared),
       "PatchTST": PatchTST(**shared), "TiDE": TiDE(**shared)}
seconds = {}
for name, model in zoo.items():
    start = time.time()
    neural = NeuralForecast(models=[model], freq="MS")
    neural.fit(train_m3)
    forecasts = forecasts.merge(neural.predict(), on=["unique_id", "ds"])
    seconds[name] = time.time() - start
```

```{python}
#| include: false
from neuralforecast import NeuralForecast
from neuralforecast.models import MLP, LSTM, GRU, TCN, DeepAR, NBEATS, NHITS, TFT, PatchTST, TiDE
from neuralforecast.losses.pytorch import DistributionLoss, MAE
import time

quiet = dict(enable_progress_bar=False, logger=False, enable_model_summary=False)
shared = dict(h=H_M3, input_size=24, scaler_type="robust", max_steps=600, random_seed=1, **quiet)
zoo = {"MLP": MLP(**shared), "LSTM": LSTM(**shared), "GRU": GRU(**shared), "TCN": TCN(**shared),
       "DeepAR": DeepAR(**shared, loss=DistributionLoss("StudentT", level=[80]), valid_loss=MAE()),
       "NBEATS": NBEATS(**shared), "NHITS": NHITS(**shared), "TFT": TFT(**shared),
       "PatchTST": PatchTST(**shared), "TiDE": TiDE(**shared)}
seconds = {}
for name, model in zoo.items():
    def train(model=model):
        start = time.time()
        neural = NeuralForecast(models=[model], freq="MS")
        neural.fit(train_m3)
        return neural.predict(), time.time() - start
    predicted, seconds[name] = cached(f"zoo-{name}", train)
    forecasts = forecasts.merge(predicted, on=["unique_id", "ds"])
```

## The zoo, scored {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| output-location: column
point = {name: name for name in zoo}
point["DeepAR"] = "DeepAR-median" if "DeepAR-median" in forecasts else "DeepAR"
board = m3_board(["snaive", "ETS", "Theta", "ETS + Theta", "LightGBM"]
                 + [point[name] for name in zoo])
board.index = [i.replace("-median", "") for i in board.index]
board["training, s (GPU)"] = pd.Series(seconds)
scoreboard(board, rules={"mean MASE": "lower", "median MASE": "lower",
                         "beats ETS on": "higher", "training, s (GPU)": "lower"}).tab_options(
    table_font_size="0.72em", data_row_padding="1px")
```

## What the table says {.smaller}

- **No network, untuned, beats ETS and Theta on M3.** The best three — N-BEATS, N-HiTS and the plain
  MLP — are level with ETS. The fully connected family wins the zoo.
- **Architecture fame is not accuracy.** PatchTST and TiDE, built for long multivariate data, are the
  two worst networks here; the LSTM loses to the plain MLP.
- **Cost differs.** On a GPU, TFT trains for 18 seconds where the MLP takes 4; on a laptop CPU the same
  gap is ten minutes against ten seconds — for a middling score.
- **The Week 8 average of ETS and Theta is still the best forecast on the board**, and it took no GPU,
  no seed and no hyperparameters.

M3 is home ground for local models: **short** series (median 115 months) from **unrelated** domains —
little for pooling to borrow. Global networks win where series are many, long and alike — M5's
products from one retailer, electricity meters, web traffic — and where someone tunes them.

## The interval DeepAR draws {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: deepar-fan
#| fig-align: center
point_col = "DeepAR-median" if "DeepAR-median" in forecasts else "DeepAR"
coverage_deepar = np.mean((forecasts["y"] >= forecasts["DeepAR-lo-80"]) & (forecasts["y"] <= forecasts["DeepAR-hi-80"]))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.2))
for ax, uid in zip(axes, ["M1143", "M484", "M1176"]):
    hist = train_m3[train_m3["unique_id"] == uid].tail(48)
    fut = forecasts[forecasts["unique_id"] == uid]
    ax.plot(hist["ds"], hist["y"], color=slate, linewidth=1)
    ax.plot(fut["ds"], fut["y"], color="black", linewidth=1, label="actual")
    ax.fill_between(fut["ds"], fut["DeepAR-lo-80"], fut["DeepAR-hi-80"], color=purple, alpha=0.2, label="DeepAR 80%")
    ax.plot(fut["ds"], fut[point_col], color=purple, linewidth=1.8, label="DeepAR median")
    ax.plot(fut["ds"], fut["ETS"], "--", color=blue, linewidth=1.3, label="ETS")
    ax.set_title(uid, fontsize=10)
axes[0].legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
fig.suptitle(f"Across all 1428 series, the 80% interval covered {coverage_deepar:.0%} of the held-out months", fontsize=11)
plt.show()
```

- **The interval is far too narrow.** A calibrated 80% interval covers 80% of the months; DeepAR's
  covers under half. On M1143 the band is narrow and misses the actual months altogether.
- **M1176:** the yearly spikes that ETS reproduces exactly are missing from both DeepAR's median and its
  band — the network smoothed them away as noise.
- A distribution in the output does not make the forecast honest. As in Week 8: **score the coverage**,
  whoever drew the interval.

## Tuning, and why we did not {.smaller}

Every model above has a dozen hyperparameters: `input_size`, layer sizes, learning rate, `max_steps`,
dropout. `neuralforecast` ships an **Auto** version of each that searches them on validation windows:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| eval: false
from neuralforecast.auto import AutoNHITS

auto = NeuralForecast(models=[AutoNHITS(h=18, backend="optuna", num_samples=20)], freq="MS")
auto.fit(train_m3, val_size=18)        # 20 configurations, each judged on the last 18 months
```

- Twenty configurations cost twenty trainings. On a laptop CPU that is the difference between a
  minute and an evening.
- The validation window must **not** be the test window — Week 3's rule, now with twenty chances to
  break it.
- Tuning is worth it when the series are many and alike, and the forecasts are used every day. For
  one series, Weeks 4–8 are cheaper and usually as good.

# Wrapping up

## Eight ways to get this wrong {.tiny}

| Trap | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| A neural network on 100 observations | A perfect fit, a wild forecast | Few weights, a global model, or a simpler model |
| One random seed | A different forecast every run | Average several networks, or fix and report the seed |
| Unscaled inputs to a network | Training that never converges | Scale each series first |
| A global model on incomparable series | Big series dominate the loss | Scale per series: `LocalStandardScaler`, `scaler_type` |
| Neural results without a benchmark | "LSTM: MAE 412" — and nothing to compare it with | Seasonal naive and ETS on the same holdout, always |
| A daily model with no lags | Loses to "same day last week" | Add the lags: AR-Net, or a model that has them |
| Tuning on the test window | A score that will not repeat | Validation windows before the test, as in Week 3 |
| "Deep" read as "better" | A slow, opaque model that loses to Theta | It is one more candidate on the rolling origin |

## What this lecture is, in one slide {.smaller}

- **NNAR** is an autoregression with a hidden layer: non-linear, local, averaged over random starts,
  with intervals by simulation. It needs long series.
- **NeuralProphet** is Prophet plus an AR-Net. On daily data the lags, not the decomposition, carry the
  accuracy — and the package itself is no longer maintained.
- **Global models** pool many series after scaling each. Every `neuralforecast` model learns from the
  same windows; they differ in how they read one — all at once (MLP, N-BEATS, N-HiTS, TiDE), step by
  step (LSTM, DeepAR), by filters (TCN) or by attention (TFT, PatchTST).
- **On M3 none of them, untuned, clearly beats ETS and Theta.** Networks earn their cost where series
  are many, long and alike — and where someone tunes them.
